theory.overview: The Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) is the first 'deep' neural network—a stack of fully-connected layers that can learn non-linear mappings from inputs to outputs. Unlike the single-layer perceptron, MLPs can solve the XOR problem and approximate any continuous function (Universal Approximation Theorem). By stacking layers with non-linear activations, MLPs learn hierarchical representations: early layers detect simple patterns, later layers combine them into complex concepts. This architecture forms the foundation for all modern deep learning.

sections.title: From Perceptron to Deep Network
sections.content: A single perceptron can only learn linear decision boundaries—it fails on XOR. The solution: stack multiple layers. The hidden layers transform the input into a space where the problem becomes linearly separable. This is the power of depth: each layer learns increasingly abstract features.
sections.universalApproximation: An MLP with one hidden layer containing sufficient neurons can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary precision.

sections.title: Layer Types in MLP
sections.content: Understanding the three layer types helps design effective architectures.

layers.name: Input Layer
layers.description: Holds the raw input features. No computation, just passes data forward.

layers.name: Hidden Layer(s)
layers.description: Transform input through learned weights and non-linear activations. This is where the magic happens.
characteristics: Number of layers = depth, neurons per layer = width

layers.name: Output Layer
layers.description: Produces final predictions. Architecture depends on task.

sections.title: Forward Pass Through MLP
sections.content: Data flows through the network layer by layer. Each layer transforms its input through linear transformation (weights) followed by non-linear activation.
sections.dimensions: If layer $l-1$ has $n$ neurons and layer $l$ has $m$ neurons, then $W^{[l]} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $b^{[l]} \in \mathbb{R}^m$.

sections.title: Designing MLP Architecture
sections.content: Choosing the right architecture is part art, part science. Key decisions: how many layers? How many neurons per layer?

guidelines.advice: 1-2 hidden layers often sufficient for tabular data
Deeper networks (more layers) learn hierarchical features; wider networks (more neurons per layer) memorize better
Input layer size = feature count; Hidden layer sizes typically between input and output
Too many parameters overfit. Use regularization, dropout, or reduce size
Decreasing layer sizes forces compression (autoencoder style)

sections.title: Training Deep MLPs
sections.content: Training MLPs requires careful initialization, proper normalization, and sometimes architectural tricks to ensure gradients flow well through deep stacks.

techniques.name: Xavier/He Initialization
techniques.purpose: Prevent vanishing/exploding gradients in deep networks

techniques.name: Batch Normalization
techniques.purpose: Stabilize training by normalizing layer inputs
techniques.benefit: Allows higher learning rates, reduces internal covariate shift

techniques.name: Residual Connections
techniques.purpose: Skip connections for very deep networks

techniques.name: Dropout
techniques.purpose: Prevent overfitting by randomly dropping neurons during training

keyConcepts.name: Depth
keyConcepts.description: Number of hidden layers. More depth enables learning hierarchical features but increases training difficulty.
keyConcepts.tradeoff: Deeper = more expressive but harder to train

keyConcepts.name: Width
keyConcepts.description: Number of neurons per layer. Wider networks have more capacity to memorize patterns.
keyConcepts.capacity: Total parameters = sum of (weights + biases) across all layers

keyConcepts.name: Feature Hierarchy
keyConcepts.description: Early layers learn simple features (edges), later layers combine them (shapes, objects).
keyConcepts.example: Vision: pixels → edges → textures → parts → objects

keyConcepts.name: Vanishing Gradients in Deep MLPs
keyConcepts.description: In very deep networks with sigmoid/tanh, gradients shrink exponentially going backward.
keyConcepts.solution: Use ReLU, batch norm, residual connections, or careful initialization

complexity.forwardPass: $O(\sum_{l=1}^L n_{l-1} \cdot n_l)$—multiply-add operations across all layers

steps.title: Define Architecture
steps.description: Choose layer sizes based on problem complexity.

steps.title: Initialize Weights
steps.description: Small random values with proper scaling (Xavier/He initialization).

steps.title: Hidden Layer Computation
steps.description: Transform input through first weight matrix and activation.

steps.title: Apply Activation
steps.description: Pass through ReLU to introduce non-linearity.

steps.title: Output Layer
steps.description: Compute final output using hidden layer activations.

steps.title: Final Activation
steps.description: Apply output activation based on task (sigmoid for binary classification).

practiceProblems.title: Parameter Count
practiceProblems.description: An MLP has layers: input (10) → hidden (20) → hidden (15) → output (5). How many total parameters?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each layer has (input_size × output_size) weights + output_size biases. Sum across all layers.

practiceProblems.title: XOR with MLP
practiceProblems.description: Design the smallest MLP that can solve XOR. Specify architecture and one valid weight configuration.
practiceProblems.answer: 2-2-1 MLP works. Example: W₁ = [[1,1],[1,1]], b₁ = [0,-1], W₂ = [1,-2], b₂ = 0. First hidden neuron acts as OR, second as AND, output subtracts them.
practiceProblems.explanation: XOR = (x₁ OR x₂) AND NOT(x₁ AND x₂). Hidden layer learns these intermediate features. Single layer can't separate XOR's non-linear boundary.
hints: One neuron learns OR, one learns AND

practiceProblems.title: Depth vs Width Trade-off
practiceProblems.description: Compare a network with [1000] (1 wide layer) vs [32, 32, 32, 32] (4 narrow layers). Both have ~1000 parameters. Which learns better?
practiceProblems.answer: The deep network [32,32,32,32] usually learns better hierarchical features and generalizes better, though both have similar capacity.
practiceProblems.explanation: Deep networks compose simple features into complex ones—early layers learn primitives, later layers combine them. Wide networks may memorize more. Empirically, depth often beats width for learning structure.

practiceProblems.title: Output Layer Design
practiceProblems.description: Specify output layer for: (a) Binary sentiment classification, (b) 10-class digit recognition, (c) House price prediction, (d] Multi-label tagging (each example can have multiple tags).
practiceProblems.answer: (a) 1 neuron, sigmoid | (b) 10 neurons, softmax | (c) 1 neuron, linear | (d) N neurons, sigmoid (independent probabilities)
practiceProblems.explanation: Binary: 1 output, probability of positive class. Multi-class: N outputs, softmax for mutually exclusive. Regression: linear for unbounded continuous. Multi-label: sigmoid per class for independent probabilities.

practiceProblems.title: Vanishing Gradient Analysis
practiceProblems.description: A 10-layer MLP uses sigmoid everywhere. Input = 5, target = 1. First forward pass: all sigmoid outputs ≈ 0.5. Estimate gradient magnitude at first layer vs last layer.
practiceProblems.answer: Last layer gradient ≈ 0.25 (max sigmoid derivative). After 9 multiplications by ≤0.25: first layer gradient ≤ 0.25^9 ≈ 3.8×10⁻⁶—essentially zero!
practiceProblems.explanation: Sigmoid derivative max is 0.25. Each layer multiplies gradient by at most 0.25 during backprop. After n layers: gradient ≤ 0.25ⁿ. This is why deep networks need ReLU, batch norm, or residual connections.

practiceProblems.title: Bottleneck Architecture
practiceProblems.description: Design an MLP for MNIST (784 inputs) that compresses to a 10-dimensional bottleneck then expands back to 784 (autoencoder). Specify layer sizes.
practiceProblems.answer: 784 → 256 → 64 → 10 → 64 → 256 → 784. Encoder: 784→256→64→10. Decoder: 10→64→256→784. Total params reasonable, learns compressed representation.
practiceProblems.explanation: Hourglass shape forces network to learn compressed representation. 10-dim bottleneck is 78× smaller than input! Network must learn most important features. Symmetric decoder reconstructs from compressed code.

minigame.title: MLP Architect
minigame.description: Design and train MLPs to solve classification problems. Adjust architecture, watch feature learning, and compete to build the most efficient network.
instructions: Select a dataset: XOR circles, spirals, or moons
Design your architecture: number of layers and neurons per layer
Watch the decision boundary evolve as the network learns
Try to use the fewest parameters while achieving high accuracy
Experiment: Deep vs Wide, different activation functions

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np

class MLP:
    """
    Multi-Layer Perceptron with configurable architecture
    Supports arbitrary layer sizes and various activation functions
    """
    def __init__(self, layer_sizes, activation='relu', output_activation='sigmoid'):
        """
        Args:
            layer_sizes: List of layer dimensions, e.g., [2, 4, 4, 1]
            activation: Activation for hidden layers ('relu', 'sigmoid', 'tanh')
            output_activation: Activation for output layer
        """
        self.layer_sizes = layer_sizes
        self.n_layers = len(layer_sizes) - 1  # excluding input
        self.activation_name = activation
        self.output_activation_name = output_activation
        
        # Initialize weights and biases with Xavier/He initialization
        self.weights = []
        self.biases = []
        
        for i in range(self.n_layers):
            n_in = layer_sizes[i]
            n_out = layer_sizes[i + 1]
            
            # Xavier initialization
            limit = np.sqrt(6.0 / (n_in + n_out))
            W = np.random.uniform(-limit, limit, (n_out, n_in))
            b = np.zeros((n_out, 1))
            
            self.weights.append(W)
            self.biases.append(b)
        
        # Cache for backprop
        self.z_values = []
        self.a_values = []
    
    def _activation(self, z, name):
        """Apply activation function"""
        if name == 'relu':
            return np.maximum(0, z)
        elif name == 'sigmoid':
            return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
        elif name == 'tanh':
            return np.tanh(z)
        elif name == 'linear':
            return z
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown activation: {name}")
    
    def _activation_derivative(self, a, z, name):
        """Compute derivative of activation"""
        if name == 'relu':
            return (z > 0).astype(float)
        elif name == 'sigmoid':
            return a * (1 - a)
        elif name == 'tanh':
            return 1 - a ** 2
        elif name == 'linear':
            return np.ones_like(z)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown activation: {name}")
    
    def forward(self, X):
        """
        Forward pass through network
        X: Input of shape (n_features, n_samples) or (n_features,)
        Returns: Output predictions
        """
        # Ensure 2D array
        if X.ndim == 1:
            X = X.reshape(-1, 1)
        
        self.z_values = []
        self.a_values = [X]  # a[0] = input
        
        a = X
        for i, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(self.weights, self.biases)):
            # Linear transformation
            z = W @ a + b
            self.z_values.append(z)
            
            # Activation
            if i == self.n_layers - 1:  # Output layer
                a = self._activation(z, self.output_activation_name)
            else:
                a = self._activation(z, self.activation_name)
            
            self.a_values.append(a)
        
        return a
    
    def backward(self, X, y, learning_rate=0.01):
        """
        Backpropagation to compute gradients and update weights
        Returns: loss value
        """
        m = y.shape[1] if y.ndim > 1 else 1  # number of examples
        
        # Forward pass
        output = self.forward(X)
        
        # Compute loss (binary cross-entropy)
        eps = 1e-8
        loss = -np.mean(y * np.log(output + eps) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - output + eps))
        
        # Backward pass
        deltas = [None] * self.n_layers
        
        # Output layer delta
        output_act = self.output_activation_name
        if output_act == 'sigmoid':
            deltas[-1] = output - y
        else:
            # General case
            da = output - y  # dL/da
            dz = da * self._activation_derivative(output, self.z_values[-1], output_act)
            deltas[-1] = dz
        
        # Hidden layers
        for l in range(self.n_layers - 2, -1, -1):
            da = self.weights[l + 1].T @ deltas[l + 1]
            dz = da * self._activation_derivative(
                self.a_values[l + 1], self.z_values[l], self.activation_name
            )
            deltas[l] = dz
        
        # Compute gradients and update
        for l in range(self.n_layers):
            dW = deltas[l] @ self.a_values[l].T / m
            db = np.mean(deltas[l], axis=1, keepdims=True)
            
            self.weights[l] -= learning_rate * dW
            self.biases[l] -= learning_rate * db
        
        return loss
    
    def train(self, X, y, epochs=1000, learning_rate=0.01, verbose=True):
        """Train the network"""
        if X.ndim == 1:
            X = X.reshape(1, -1)
        if y.ndim == 1:
            y = y.reshape(1, -1)
        
        losses = []
        
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            loss = self.backward(X, y, learning_rate)
            losses.append(loss)
            
            if verbose and epoch % 100 == 0:
                print(f"Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {loss:.4f}")
        
        return losses
    
    def predict(self, X):
        """Make predictions"""
        output = self.forward(X)
        return (output > 0.5).astype(int)
    
    def get_parameters(self):
        """Return total number of parameters"""
        total = 0
        for W, b in zip(self.weights, self.biases):
            total += W.size + b.size
        return total

# ==================== Examples ====================

def demo_xor():
    """Classic XOR problem - requires hidden layer"""
    print("\n=== XOR Problem Demo ===")
    
    # XOR dataset
    X = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 1],
                  [0, 1, 0, 1]])  # shape: (2, 4)
    y = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0]])  # shape: (1, 4)
    
    # Create MLP: 2 inputs -> 4 hidden -> 1 output
    mlp = MLP([2, 4, 1], activation='relu', output_activation='sigmoid')
    
    print(f"Architecture: {mlp.layer_sizes}")
    print(f"Total parameters: {mlp.get_parameters()}")
    
    # Train
    losses = mlp.train(X, y, epochs=5000, learning_rate=0.5)
    
    # Test
    print("\nPredictions after training:")
    for i in range(4):
        pred = mlp.forward(X[:, i].reshape(2, 1))
        print(f"  X=[{X[0,i]},{X[1,i]}]: prediction={pred[0,0]:.4f}, target={y[0,i]}")

def demo_classification():
    """2D classification with visualization"""
    print("\n=== 2D Classification Demo ===")
    
    # Generate spiral data
    def generate_spiral(n_points, n_classes=3):
        X = np.zeros((2, n_points * n_classes))
        y = np.zeros((1, n_points * n_classes))
        
        for class_num in range(n_classes):
            ix = range(n_points * class_num, n_points * (class_num + 1))
            r = np.linspace(0, 1, n_points)
            t = np.linspace(class_num * 4, (class_num + 1) * 4, n_points) + np.random.randn(n_points) * 0.2
            X[:, ix] = np.c_[r * np.sin(t), r * np.cos(t)].T
            y[:, ix] = class_num
        
        return X, y
    
    # For simplicity, use a 2-class problem
    # Concentric circles
    n = 100
    theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, n)
    r1 = np.random.randn(n) * 0.1 + 0.5
    r2 = np.random.randn(n) * 0.1 + 1.5
    
    X_inner = np.array([r1 * np.cos(theta), r1 * np.sin(theta)])
    X_outer = np.array([r2 * np.cos(theta), r2 * np.sin(theta)])
    X = np.hstack([X_inner, X_outer])
    y = np.hstack([np.zeros((1, n)), np.ones((1, n))])
    
    # Create and train MLP
    mlp = MLP([2, 8, 8, 1], activation='relu', output_activation='sigmoid')
    print(f"Architecture: {mlp.layer_sizes}")
    print(f"Total parameters: {mlp.get_parameters()}")
    
    losses = mlp.train(X, y, epochs=2000, learning_rate=0.1)
    
    # Evaluate
    predictions = mlp.predict(X)
    accuracy = np.mean(predictions == y)
    print(f"Final accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")

def compare_architectures():
    """Compare different architectures on the same problem"""
    print("\n=== Architecture Comparison ===")
    
    # XOR problem
    X = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1]])
    y = np.array([[0, 1, 1, 0]])
    
    architectures = [
        [2, 1],      # No hidden layer (should fail)
        [2, 2, 1],   # Minimal hidden layer
        [2, 4, 1],   # Standard
        [2, 8, 8, 1] # Deep
    ]
    
    for arch in architectures:
        mlp = MLP(arch, activation='relu', output_activation='sigmoid')
        mlp.train(X, y, epochs=3000, learning_rate=0.5, verbose=False)
        
        # Test accuracy
        preds = [mlp.forward(X[:, i].reshape(2, 1))[0, 0] for i in range(4)]
        correct = sum((p > 0.5) == y[0, i] for i, p in enumerate(preds))
        
        print(f"{str(arch):20s}: {correct}/4 correct, {mlp.get_parameters()} params")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_xor()
    demo_classification()
    compare_architectures()
    
    print("\n=== Key Insights ===")
    print("1. XOR requires at least one hidden layer")
    print("2. ReLU typically trains faster than sigmoid")
    print("3. Proper initialization (Xavier/He) is crucial for deep networks")
    print("4. Architecture choice balances capacity vs. generalization")
